questions.question: What are len and cap of a slice in Go, and how are they related?
questions.title: Re Len And Cap Of A Slice
questions.direct_answer: len is how many elements the slice can see right now; cap is how many slots exist in the backing array. Appends below cap never allocate; at cap, append reallocates and roughly doubles.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: len is how many elements the slice can see right now; cap is how many slots exist in the backing array. Appends below cap never allocate; at cap, append reallocates and roughly doubles.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A slice is a header with three fields: a pointer to the start of its elements, a length, and a capacity. The length is what you iterate over — `for i := 0; i < len(s); i++` and what `range` covers. The capacity is the size of the underlying array from the slice's start — the total room the slice can grow into before the runtime has to move it.

They differ the moment you re-slice: `t := s[:2]` on a 3-element slice gives len 2 but cap 3, because the backing array still has that third slot. That gap is exactly what append exploits — appending to t writes into the spare slot in place.

When len reaches cap, the next append allocates a new, larger backing array (roughly double for small slices), copies the elements, and the slice header now points at the new storage. Old aliases to the previous array don't see the growth — they've forked.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The len/cap split exists because slices are windows over arrays, not owned storage. The backing array is a fixed-size allocation; the slice header is a lens over it:

```
s := make([]int, 2, 4)

backing array: [ _ _ _ _ ]   (4 slots allocated)
s: ptr ──▶ [ 0 0 ]           len 2 — what s can see
                          cap 4 — total room from ptr
```

Every slice operation is defined on these two numbers. Indexing checks against len (index 2 of len-2 slice panics even though slot 2 physically exists). Append checks against cap. Re-slicing recomputes both within the cap budget: `s[2:4]` on a cap-4 slice is legal even for a len-2 slice, because the window arithmetic works on the underlying array's extent.

This is also why cap is a performance property and len is a correctness property: exceeding len is a bug the runtime catches (panic); exceeding cap is just an allocation the runtime handles. Code that pre-sizes with `make([]T, 0, n)` is aligning cap with the expected len so the appends never pay the copy.

questions.question: What is the internal structure of a Go slice?
questions.title: Internal Structure Of A Go Slice
questions.direct_answer: Three words: a pointer to the backing array's start, the length, and the capacity. Copying a slice copies this header — the elements stay shared.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Slice Internals Len Cap.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Three words: a pointer to the backing array's start, the length, and the capacity. Copying a slice copies this header — the elements stay shared.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
At the machine level a slice is a small struct — pointer, length, capacity — passed around by value. The elements live elsewhere, in a separate array the header points into. That's the whole trick behind slice behavior.

When you assign or pass a slice, those three words get copied. The new header has the same pointer, so both slices view the same elements — a write through one is visible through the other. When you append and there's capacity spare, the write goes into that shared array, and any slice with a window over the slot sees it.

This is why slice behavior feels inconsistent to newcomers: assignment shares, but growth forks. It's not inconsistent — it's a pointer-with-bounds that grows by getting a new pointer. Every surprise is one of those two facts surfacing.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
You can watch the header be three words with unsafe or with the reflect package, but the behavior demonstrates it more usefully:

```go
s := []int{1, 2, 3}
t := s                // header copied — same backing array
t[0] = 100
fmt.Println(s[0])      // 100 — shared storage

u := append(s, 4)     // s is at cap (3/3): must reallocate
s[0] = 200
fmt.Println(u[0])      // 100 — u forked to new storage
```

The first print shows sharing (header copy, same pointer). The second shows forking: append at capacity allocated a new array, copied the elements, and returned a header pointing at the new one. s's header still points at the old array, so s[0] = 200 doesn't touch u.

This is also the mechanism behind Q1's len/cap facts and every 'why did my slice change' bug in Go — they're all header semantics. The array itself never moves until an append forces it; only headers are copied, and only growth reallocates.

questions.question: How does append grow a slice internally?
questions.title: Es Append Grow A Slice Internally
questions.direct_answer: If len < cap, append writes into the spare slot — no allocation. At len == cap, it allocates a bigger array (~2x small slices), copies, and returns the new header. The result must be reassigned.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Slice Internals Len Cap.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: If len < cap, append writes into the spare slot — no allocation. At len == cap, it allocates a bigger array (~2x small slices), copies, and returns the new header. The result must be reassigned.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Append has exactly two modes. With capacity spare, it's a store: write the element at index len, bump len, return the same header. No allocation, no copy — and critically, every slice sharing that backing array sees the change.

At capacity, append grows: allocate a new array (roughly double the current capacity for small slices — a 3-cap slice grows to 6), copy the existing elements over, append the new one, and return a header pointing at the new storage. The old array is abandoned — slices still viewing it are now forked and won't see the new element or any future changes.

Because append can go either way, its return value is the only reliable handle: `s = append(s, x)`. When growth happened, the returned header points at the new array; ignoring the return keeps using the old, stale header and silently drops elements.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The doubling strategy is the classic amortized-constant trick from dynamic arrays: appending n elements with naive 1-slot growth costs O(n²) total copies; doubling means each element is copied O(1) times on average. Go tapers the factor for very large slices (where 2x over-allocates gigabytes) but small slices get ~2x.

You can observe both modes with cap prints:

```go
s := make([]int, 0, 3)      // cap 3 from the start
s = append(s, 1)           // fits: cap still 3
s = append(s, 2)           // fits: cap still 3
s = append(s, 3)           // fits exactly: cap still 3
s = append(s, 4)           // full: new array, cap now 6
fmt.Println(len(s), cap(s)) // 4 6
```

The gotcha this mechanism creates: append below capacity mutates shared state. `t := s[:2]; t = append(t, 42)` writes into s's backing array if the slot exists — s sees a changed element it never touched. That's not a bug in append; it's the in-place mode doing exactly what it's for. The fix when sharing isn't wanted is a real copy (`make + copy` or `append(nil, s...)`), which forces the allocate-mode behavior on purpose.

questions.question: Why does printing a slice show different values than expected after a sub-slice and append?
questions.title: Es Printing A Slice Show Different Values
questions.direct_answer: Because a sub-slice shares the backing array. t := s[:2]; append(t, 42) writes 42 into the third slot of the SAME array — s sees [1 2 42] even though you never touched s directly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Slice Internals Len Cap.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Because a sub-slice shares the backing array. t := s[:2]; append(t, 42) writes 42 into the third slot of the SAME array — s sees [1 2 42] even though you never touched s directly.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
This is the single most common Go data bug, and it's always the same mechanism. `t := s[:2]` creates a new header pointing at the same array — len 2, cap still 3, so there's a spare slot. `append(t, 42)` has capacity available, so it takes the in-place path: write 42 at index 2, bump t's len to 3.

Index 2 of the backing array is s's third element. s still has len 3, so when you print it, the runtime shows the array — which now contains 42. You never called append on s, never assigned s anywhere — but s changed, because s was never a copy. It was a window, and the write happened through another window onto the same room.

The fix when this is unwanted: give t its own storage before appending — `t := make([]T, len, cap); copy(t, s[:2])`, or the idiom `append([]T(nil), s[:2]...)` — so append's growth-or-in-place decision happens on t's own array, not s's.

questions.question: What is the zero value of a slice and what operations work on it?
questions.title: Zero Value Of A Slice And What
questions.direct_answer: nil. You can len it (0), range it (no iterations), append to it (allocates), and delete-free operations are fine. Only indexing panics — and writing to a nil map's sibling panic is different: nil slice writes work via append.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Slice Internals Len Cap.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: nil. You can len it (0), range it (no iterations), append to it (allocates), and delete-free operations are fine. Only indexing panics — and writing to a nil map's sibling panic is different: nil slice writes work via append.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A declared-but-unassigned slice is nil — the header's pointer is null, len and cap zero. But unlike a nil map, which panics on writes, a nil slice is mostly usable:

len(nil-slice) is 0, cap is 0. Ranging over it executes zero iterations — loop bodies just don't run. Append works, and it's not a special case: appending to a zero-cap slice takes the allocate path (there's no room), so `var s []int; s = append(s, x)` behaves exactly like starting from `[]int{}`. JSON marshals it as null (that's the visible difference from an empty-but-non-nil slice, and it matters for APIs).

What you cannot do: index into it — `s[0]` on a nil slice panics with index out of range, same as any over-index. And functions that check `if s == nil` for emptiness will distinguish nil from empty; for most purposes `len(s) == 0` is the correct emptiness test because it covers both.
